title: Software Development & Lifecycle
description: Understand what software teams build, the development lifecycle, changing requirements, engineering evidence, and what finished means.

lessons.title: Software solves a defined problem
lessons.principle: A program transforms inputs and state into observable behavior for a user or another system.
lessons.practice: Describe one user, one problem, and one measurable outcome before choosing technology.

lessons.title: Map a real task to software
lessons.principle: A useful application has actors, inputs, actions, stored information, and outcomes.
lessons.practice: For a task tracker, identify who adds tasks, what fields are stored, and what counts as completing a task.

lessons.title: Software is more than code
lessons.principle: Documentation, tests, configuration, data, interfaces, and operations are part of a usable software product.
lessons.practice: List all artifacts needed to run, verify, maintain, and recover a small application.

lessons.title: Avoid the one-file illusion
lessons.principle: An isolated code sample is not a shipped product without deployment, access, data handling, and support.
lessons.practice: Ask AI for missing delivery artifacts, then check each suggestion against the actual deployment target.

lessons.title: The software development lifecycle
lessons.principle: Discovery, planning, design, implementation, verification, release, and maintenance form an iterative lifecycle.
lessons.practice: State the deliverable and decision at each phase for a simple feature.

lessons.title: Trace a feature end to end
lessons.principle: Every feature should connect a user need to a design choice, code change, test, and release result.
lessons.practice: Follow a login feature from requirement through threat review and tests to a deployable release.

lessons.title: Roles and ownership
lessons.principle: Product, design, engineering, testing, security, and operations contribute distinct viewpoints, even on a small team.
lessons.practice: Assign an explicit owner for requirements, code review, user acceptance, and incident response.

lessons.title: AI is an assistant, not an owner
lessons.principle: A model can help with many roles but cannot independently accept organizational accountability.
lessons.practice: Name the human who approves scope, sensitive data use, merges, and production changes.

lessons.title: Iterative development
lessons.principle: Short inspect-build-verify loops reduce uncertainty and surface mistakes before they spread.
lessons.practice: Build the smallest end-to-end usable slice rather than generating the entire application in one pass.

lessons.title: A vertical slice example
lessons.principle: One complete task-creation flow reveals UI, state, storage, and error-handling integration.
lessons.practice: Implement create-task before adding search, sharing, notifications, or analytics.

lessons.title: Source, runtime, and dependencies
lessons.principle: Source files are inputs to tools and runtimes; libraries and configuration affect the resulting behavior.
lessons.practice: Identify how your program starts and which installed packages it needs.

lessons.title: Read a project before running it
lessons.principle: A repository can execute scripts that change data or contact external services.
lessons.practice: Inspect README, package scripts, environment requirements, and dependency sources before running suggested commands.

lessons.title: Evidence versus confidence
lessons.principle: A plausible explanation or generated screen is weaker evidence than tests and observed behavior.
lessons.practice: Replace claims such as 'it works' with named reproducible checks.

lessons.title: Build an evidence ladder
lessons.principle: Syntax checks, unit tests, integration tests, and user-flow tests answer different questions.
lessons.practice: Record the command, environment, result, and unresolved risk for each claim of correctness.

lessons.title: Engineering tradeoffs
lessons.principle: Time, scope, reliability, security, accessibility, and maintainability constrain one another.
lessons.practice: Discuss tradeoffs explicitly and reject improvements that damage non-negotiable requirements.

lessons.title: Compare two implementation options
lessons.principle: A local-only prototype and a hosted multi-user app have different storage, auth, and operating costs.
lessons.practice: Write a decision note that states constraints, selected approach, alternatives, and expected consequences.

lessons.title: Risk and reversibility
lessons.principle: Changes differ in impact, exposure, cost to reverse, and possible harm.
lessons.practice: Increase review depth for authentication, financial logic, destructive migrations, and privacy-sensitive paths.

lessons.title: Design a rollback before deployment
lessons.principle: A rollback plan must account for persistent data and external side effects, not only source code.
lessons.practice: For a schema change, document compatibility, backups, and what can safely be undone.

lessons.title: Definition of done
lessons.principle: A feature is complete when agreed behavior is verified and its operational obligations are satisfied.
lessons.practice: Include acceptance tests, documentation, accessibility, and release checks in the completion criteria.

lessons.title: Use a feature completion gate
lessons.principle: Merge readiness is different from deployment readiness and from user acceptance.
lessons.practice: Show the demonstrated outcome, passing checks, reviewed diff, and any known limitations before marking work done.
